narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this predicted failure rate is so high, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average ranking of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking was the third most important factor and similarly pulled the prediction toward failure; again, a bottom-decile performance contrasts sharply with the much stronger average ranking of accepted students.

Your LSAT score of 26 was the second most important factor and also increased the likelihood of failure. It sits well below the average score of 37 among admitted students.

None of the other details in your profile, such as your undergraduate GPA, family income, or plan to attend full-time, played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach a score closer to the mid-30s or higher. Stronger grades and test results in a future application would likely change the model’s prediction and open the door to admission. (218 words)
